opus-5.5.text:
I think it's sustainable, but only if we change how we think about it. Right now a lot of the field relies on teleoperation: you put a skilled operator behind a VR headset or a leader arm, and they drive the robot through a task over and over. That gives you very high-quality, embodiment-matched data, but it's expensive, slow, and it doesn't scale linearly with ambition. Every new robot, every new environment, you pay that cost again. If the plan is to collect our way to general-purpose robots purely through teleop, I'm skeptical that the economics work out.

So what's the alternative? I see a few threads coming together. One is making data collection more decoupled from the robot itself. Things like handheld grippers or wearable devices, where a person just goes about doing the task naturally and you capture the motion and the visual context. You lose a bit of fidelity, but you gain enormously in throughput and diversity, and you can collect in homes, kitchens, warehouses, places you'd never haul a robot into.

The second thread, and this is one I'm personally very excited about, is learning from ordinary human behavior, like egocentric video of people cooking, cleaning, assembling things. Humans generate an enormous amount of this kind of data just by living. The challenge is the embodiment gap: human hands aren't robot grippers, and video doesn't come with action labels. But the models are getting much better at extracting the structure of a task, the intent, the object interactions, and then grounding that on a robot with a relatively small amount of robot-specific data.

The third piece is simulation and generative models filling in the long tail, so human data provides the anchor and the semantics, and synthetic data provides the coverage.

So my view is: human data isn't going away. It's actually the most important ingredient, because it encodes what people actually want robots to do. But the way we collect it has to shift from "humans laboring to control robots" toward "robots learning from the way humans naturally act in the world." If we get that right, the data pipeline becomes something that grows almost for free, and that's when I think things really take off.

r001.rationale: The response discusses whether human-data collection can scale and how to improve it, but does not say that people’s willingness to contribute depends on continued progress in the field.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I'll be honest, I have mixed feelings about it, and I think the field does too.

The optimistic case is pretty clear. Teleoperation has gotten dramatically cheaper and easier in the last few years. Setups like ALOHA, or the various VR and leader-arm rigs, mean you no longer need a PhD student babysitting a robot for every demonstration. You can hire people, put them in front of a kit, and collect hours of data a day. And we've seen with things like Open X-Embodiment that pooling data across labs and embodiments actually helps. So there's a real path where you scale this up the way people scaled web crawls for language models, just with humans in the loop instead of scraping.

But I think that analogy breaks down in a few important places, and that's where my skepticism comes in.

First, the economics are fundamentally different. Internet text was a byproduct of billions of people doing other things. Nobody paid for it. Robot demonstrations are purpose-built, and every hour costs real money and real human attention. So the question becomes who pays for it and why, and the answer right now is mostly a handful of well-funded companies and a few large academic consortia. That's not nothing, but it's not the kind of organic, self-sustaining pipeline that language models enjoyed.

Second, the data doesn't age well. Demonstrations are tied to a specific robot, a specific gripper, a specific camera placement, often a specific lab. When your hardware changes, and it always changes, a surprising fraction of that data becomes much less useful. So you're not just collecting once, you're collecting repeatedly, and that compounds the cost problem.

Third, and this is the thing I worry about most as someone who thinks a lot about task structure, human demonstrations are actually a pretty narrow slice of what we want robots to learn. They show you one way to do a task, usually a clean one. They don't show you how to recover when you knock something over, or what to do when the drawer is stuck. The long tail is exactly where the robots fail, and it's exactly where human demos are the most expensive to collect because you have to deliberately stage failures.

So where does that leave us? I don't think human data collection goes away. I think it becomes one ingredient among several. You use high-quality human demonstrations as a seed, almost like a curriculum anchor. Then you lean on things that scale better: simulation, where we've gotten much better at generating diverse scenes and tasks; autonomous data collection, where the robot practices on its own and you filter for success; and increasingly, video of humans doing things in the world, which is abundant and free even if it's harder to use directly.

The research question I find most exciting is really about leverage. How many hours of expensive human data do you actually need if you have good priors, good structure, and good self-improvement loops around it? My bet is the answer is a lot less than people assume right now, and that the labs who figure out that ratio are the ones who'll make robot learning actually sustainable rather than just well-funded.

r001.rationale: The response discusses the cost and sustainability of collecting robot data, but does not state that people's willingness to contribute depends on the field continuing to make progress.

astra-6.text:
I think human data will continue to be important, but the question is how much human effort we need for each improvement in the robot. If every new task or environment requires another round of demonstrations at the same scale, that’s going to be difficult to sustain.

The more promising approach is to make the collection process increasingly targeted. A robot can attempt a task, identify where it struggles, and ask a person for help at those moments. Then the human is providing information the system actually needs, rather than repeating something it already knows how to do.

So I see human data as part of a broader learning loop, alongside autonomous experience. The key is whether the data we collect today helps robots learn more efficiently tomorrow. If it does, continued human involvement can be very valuable without having to grow at the same rate as the robot fleet.

r001.rationale: The response discusses making human-data collection more efficient and sustainable, but does not state that people’s willingness to contribute depends on whether the field continues making progress.

sol-6.1.text:
I think human data is going to remain an important part of robot learning, but the question is how we make collecting it sustainable. If every improvement requires someone to spend more hours teleoperating a robot, that’s a pretty expensive loop to maintain.

One direction is to make that interaction useful in itself. A person helps a robot complete a real task, and that intervention also becomes training data. Then, as the robot becomes more capable, people can focus on the difficult cases rather than demonstrating everything repeatedly.

I also think we should distinguish human video from data collected directly on a robot. Video can show what people do and give us a lot of diversity, but it doesn’t automatically tell a robot how to make contact or control its own body. So I see these sources as complementary. The goal is to learn more from each demonstration and gradually reduce how much additional human effort we need.

r001.rationale: The response discusses making data collection sustainable and reducing human effort as robots improve, but it does not say that people’s willingness to contribute depends on continued progress in the field.
